title: How to Improve Face Tracking and Hair Masks in Claude Video Effects Skills
summary:
If a Claude video effects skill cuts you out of a talking-head clip, and your face or hair looks wrong the moment you turn your head, the mask is usually the problem, not the typography. Most of these skills use a general person segmenter plus a simple face box. That is enough to put a title behind you when you are still, and a weak hair matte once you move. Keep soft alpha in the hair, track the head without letting the mask lag, and stop treating face tracking and background removal as one operation.

How Claude video effects skills actually cut you out

Claude Motion and most claude motion graphics are code-drawn animations, with nobody on camera. The Instagram-style skill packs do a different job: you drop in a talking-head video, Claude Code runs an effect such as /effects backdrop-word, and the renderer tries to sit graphics behind your head.

In the public source for Vibha Ramprakash's popular /effects skill (51 starter effects, credits in the README), that cut-out is built like this:

  1. Your clip is the input, not a text prompt.
  2. A first pass looks at the frames inside each effect window.
  3. MediaPipe Selfie Segmenter produces a person confidence mask, in video mode.
  4. A guided filter refines that mask against the grayscale frame.
  5. OpenCV YuNet detects a face box. If detection misses, the skill falls back to the top of the person mask.
  6. A second pass composites the effect. Layers marked to sit behind you are hidden wherever the person mask is opaque. The original audio is kept, and the output is an MP4, 1080p by default.

HyperFrames-based packs do the same job with npx hyperframes remove-background subject.mp4 -o subject.webm, plus --background-output plate.webm if you want type behind the person. Claude is driving this pipeline; it is not generating the footage.

Why the mask looks worse when you move

Three details in that public /effects tracker explain the usual failure, especially around hair.

First, Selfie Segmenter is a person segmenter, not a hair-aware matte. Fine strands against a busy background are already at the edge of what this class of model keeps. HyperFrames' own guide says the same about its local model: expect trouble with fine hair and fast motion, and the softer hair edges are often the model's limit on that source.

Second, after the guided filter, the skill hardens the mask with a contrast stretch around 0.5. That helps a clean silhouette, but it pushes semi-transparent hair toward fully foreground or fully background. The edge can look wig-like, or a chunk of hair can appear and disappear when you turn.

Third, the mask is only blended one way with the previous frame. Face boxes later get a bidirectional smooth so the box does not lag; the matte does not. A one-way blend can smear on a quick turn, and the previous mask is cleared outside an effect window, so the first frame of a new effect can jump.

YuNet also gives a box, not a head pose. When you turn, the visible face shape changes, and a guard drawn around the box center will not match. The analysis runs on a downscaled frame (around 540 pixels on the short side) and is then scaled up, which throws away the pixels you need for hair.

Fix the source before you rewrite the skill

A better matte still needs a clip the model can read.

  • Use a plain background that contrasts with your hair, not a busy wall or a similar color.
  • Keep the framing steady, leave space around your head, and prefer the vertical phone video this skill is built for.
  • Light the face and the hair edge. Backlight helps strands read as hair instead of noise.
  • Slow the head motion in the takes you care about. Fast turns are a documented failure case for these local cut-out models.
  • Watch dark objects you hold: a mic or phone can be swallowed by a people-only model. HyperFrames documents this limit.
  • Use the skill's check-frame pass before you encode. It writes a plan, renders stills at the middle of each effect, then encodes. If a still already shows a hole in your hair, the render will too.

Separate tracking from the hair matte

Once the source is cleaner, change the mask logic. The following is illustrative, based on the public skill source. It is not a patch I have run, and it is not an online implementation.

Keep the guided filter, which already aligns the matte with image edges. What usually hurts hair is the hardening after it. Leave soft alpha around 0.5 instead of stretching every pixel to 0 or 1:

# Illustrative only. m is the confidence mask after the guided filter.
m = np.clip(m, 0, 1)
# Keep a soft band for hair; do not apply a contrast stretch around 0.5.
hair_band = (m > 0.2) & (m < 0.8)

For flicker, smooth the boundary jitter, not the head motion. The skill already applies a no-lag, bidirectional smooth to the face box. A similar idea can go on the matte edge, so the silhouette can still follow a quick turn. Do not clear the previous mask just because you left an effect window for a few frames.

If you only need the official HyperFrames cut-out, try --quality best when the cut-out goes back over its own footage (this reduces a color halo), and a cleaner source or a stronger external matte when edges flicker. The plate from --background-output is a person-shaped hole, not an inpainted background. Stack something opaque under it.

Do not reshape the hair matte from the YuNet box center alone. If you change tracking, add landmarks or a head-pose estimate to the already-smoothed box. And if you can afford the time, run the segmenter closer to output resolution. A 540-pixel matte cannot invent strands that were never in the analysis frame.

A prompt you can paste into Claude Code

If you are working with the /effects skill on your machine, you can ask Claude Code to adjust the tracker rather than rebuilding the pipeline. Adapt this:

The cut-out in this Claude video effects skill looks uneven on my hair when I turn my head.

Please inspect scripts/fx.py (the Tracker, the guided filter, and the mask hardening).
Do not treat this as a one-click production patch. Propose a small, reversible change that:

1. Keeps the MediaPipe Selfie Segmenter and the guided filter.
2. Stops hardening the mask with a strong contrast stretch around 0.5, so hair can keep soft alpha.
3. Smooths mask-edge flicker without making the matte lag behind a quick head turn. Reuse the idea behind the existing bidirectional face-box smooth.
4. Does not clear the previous mask between nearby effect windows.
5. Optionally runs the segmenter closer to the output resolution, and says what that will cost in time.
6. Leaves YuNet in place for the face box, but does not use the box center alone to reshape the hair matte.

Show me the diff first. Then render check-frame stills, not the full MP4, so I can inspect the hair edge.

Watch the stills before you post. The skill's own README calls these starter versions, and asks you to approve the draft.

When you do not need a talking-head cut-out

If the clip you want is type, charts, or a product interface, and nobody has to be filmed, this masking problem does not apply. That is the other branch of claude motion graphics: Claude writes animation code, and a renderer makes the MP4. Anthropic's official Claude Motion feature works that way, on Team and Enterprise plans, and it does not generate footage of real people.

I maintain Opus 5.5 Video, a browser-based Claude Motion alternative for that no-install path. It is an independent site, not affiliated with Anthropic, and it will not fix a talking-head mask: it does not accept a video upload or cut people out of footage. Use it only for a prompt-to-1080p motion-graphics MP4, at 15, 30, or 60 seconds. For a filmed speaker with graphics behind their head, stay on the skill-and-matte path above.

A short checklist

  • Confirm you are on the talking-head branch, not a code-only claude animation.
  • Relight and recrop the source before you blame the model.
  • Inspect check-frame stills, especially during a head turn, before you encode.
  • Keep soft hair alpha; do not harden the whole person into a sticker.
  • Stabilize edge flicker, not the actual motion of the head.
  • Treat YuNet as a box, not as a pose.
  • If you use HyperFrames, try --quality best for a halo, and a stronger matte only after the source is clean.
  • If you do not need a person in the frame, skip background removal entirely.

title: How to monitor Polish public tenders (BZP) and see who won with Python
summary:
Polish public procurement is a big, open data source that most sales teams outside Poland never touch. Every tender below the EU thresholds goes into the Biuletyn Zamówień Publicznych (BZP), run by the Public Procurement Office (UZP) on the eZamówienia platform. The search interface works fine for a person checking one category once a week. It gets painful when you want a daily feed for a few CPV codes, or when you want to know who won and at what price.

This tutorial uses the Poland Public Tenders Scraper on Apify. It reads the official UZP API, filters by CPV code, keyword, region and buyer, and for award notices it opens the full notice PDF to pull out the winning contract price.

I ran it on Monday 23 November 2026 for CPV 72000000 (IT services) with a 7-day window. All numbers below come from that run.

What the run returned

30 records in total:

  • 17 new contract notices (open tenders)
  • 12 award notices (11 "contract signed", 1 "contract signed, partially")
  • 1 cancellation

Buyers came from all over the country. Śląskie had 6 records, Mazowieckie and Dolnośląskie 4 each, Świętokrzyskie 3. The buyers were what you would expect for IT services: hospitals, universities, municipal water companies, fire service units and city halls. Kraków city hall was looking for a DLP system. A Wrocław IT service centre wanted SAP support and development.

For the 9 awards where the scraper fetched a contract price, the values ranged from 159,900 PLN to 1,097,900 PLN net, with a median of 568,014 PLN. Together that is about 4.65 million PLN of signed IT work in one week, from the subset that got enriched.

Deadlines were short. All 17 open tenders had between 3 and 8 days left to submit an offer. If you check BZP by hand once a week, you will miss some of them.

Price still dominates evaluation. 12 notices had parsed criteria: 7 used price at 60% (the rest split between things like repair time and response time), and 5 used price as the only criterion at 100%.

Fields you get

One notice is one record. The most useful fields:

Field What it contains
eventType new, changed, awarded or cancelled
noticeNumber, bzpNumber Official BZP identifiers
publicationDate When the notice was published (UTC)
orderObject Subject of the contract, in Polish
cpvCodes, cpvNames CPV codes with Polish names
organizationName, organizationCity, organizationProvinceName The contracting authority
organizationNip, organizationRegon Tax ID and statistical ID of the buyer
submittingOffersDate, daysToDeadline Offer deadline and days left
procedureResultLabel Outcome for award notices
contractors Winners with city, IDs and contractPrice
contractValueNet, contractValueDisplay Winning contract value
evaluationCriteria Criteria with weights, from the PDF
estimatedValueNet, estimatedValueAvailable Estimated value, when the buyer published it
documentsAvailable in-notice, on-platform-only or none
sourceUrl, pdfUrl Links to the notice on eZamówienia

Two things to know before you build on this. First, estimatedValueAvailable was true for only 1 of the 30 records, because all of them were below EU thresholds and those notices rarely publish an estimate. The award price is the number you can rely on. Second, tender documents (SWZ and attachments) live on the eZamówienia platform, so 17 records said on-platform-only and 13 said none. Use sourceUrl to get them.

Option 1: no code

  1. Open the actor page and click Try for free.
  2. In CPV codes, enter the categories you sell into. Matching is hierarchical, so 72000000 also catches 72200000, 72222300 and the rest of the IT tree. Other common roots: 48000000 (software), 45000000 (construction), 33000000 (medical), 79000000 (business and legal services).
  3. Optionally add keywords. They match the title by default, ignoring case and Polish diacritics, so bezpieczenstwo finds "Bezpieczeństwo".
  4. Optionally filter by voivodeships (names like Mazowieckie or codes like PL14) and by contracting authority (part of a name, a 10-digit NIP or a REGON).
  5. Pick notice types. The default is new tenders plus awards. You can add plans, concessions, competitions and corrections.
  6. Set mode. For a first look use "all matching". For a scheduled monitor keep the default "new or changed only".
  7. Click Start and export the dataset as CSV, Excel or JSON.

The input form labels are in Polish, but each field has a description, and the JSON tab accepts the English keys shown below.

Input options that matter

  • dateLookbackDays: publication window, 1 to 30 days. Default 7.
  • mode: new_only remembers what it already returned under a stateKey and only sends new or changed notices next time. all returns everything in the window.
  • stateKey: the memory slot for new_only. If you change filters, use a new key. Otherwise the actor skips anything older than your last run and you can get 0 results.
  • enrichWithDetails: downloads the notice PDF for criteria, conditions and estimated value. On by default.
  • enrichAwardsWithPrice: pulls the winning price for awards. On by default.
  • enrichMaxPerRun: cost cap on PDF downloads per run, default 50. I set it to 20, which is why only 9 of the 12 awards got a price. Newest notices go first.
  • matchInFullText: also search keywords in the full notice text instead of the title only. Costs extra per notice.
  • minAwardPriceNet / maxAwardPriceNet: filter awards by contract value in PLN.

Option 2: Python with apify-client and pandas

Install the two libraries:

pip install apify-client pandas

This is the same input I used, plus a few lines to split open tenders from awards:

from apify_client import ApifyClient
import pandas as pd

client = ApifyClient("YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN")

run_input = {
    "cpvCodes": ["72000000"],
    "noticeTypes": ["contract", "award"],
    "mode": "all",
    "dateLookbackDays": 7,
    "stateKey": "it-tenders-test",
    "enrichWithDetails": True,
    "enrichAwardsWithPrice": True,
    "enrichMaxPerRun": 20,
}

run = client.actor("liveclaude/bzp-monitor-pl").call(run_input=run_input)
items = list(client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items())
df = pd.DataFrame(items)

print(df["eventType"].value_counts())

# Open tenders, closest deadline first
open_tenders = (
    df[df["eventType"] == "new"]
    [["daysToDeadline", "organizationName", "organizationProvinceName",
      "orderObject", "sourceUrl"]]
    .sort_values("daysToDeadline")
)
print(open_tenders.head(10).to_string(index=False))

# Awards with a known contract value
awards = df[(df["eventType"] == "awarded") & df["contractValueNet"].notna()]
print(awards["contractValueNet"].describe())

# Which buyers spend the most
by_buyer = (
    awards.groupby("organizationName")["contractValueNet"]
    .sum()
    .sort_values(ascending=False)
)
print(by_buyer.head(10))

open_tenders.to_csv("open_it_tenders.csv", index=False)

The contractors column is a list of dicts. If you want one row per winner, use pd.json_normalize(items, record_path="contractors", meta=["bzpNumber", "organizationName"]). Keep in mind the note on personal data further down before you store or share that table.

Scheduling and integrations

For a monitor, switch mode to new_only, give the search a fixed stateKey, and add a schedule in Apify (Schedules tab). Daily at 7:00 works for most teams. With a 3 to 8 day window to respond, I would not go less often than daily.

Then route the output somewhere people already look:

  • A webhook to Slack or Teams when a run finishes with new items
  • Make or Zapier to create a CRM deal per new tender
  • A Google Sheets export for a shared tender list
  • The Apify API from your own backend, as in the Python example

Pricing

The actor uses pay-per-event pricing, so you pay for notices found and PDFs parsed, not for scanning. Current prices on the Free plan, per 1,000 events:

Event Free plan Gold plan
New matching notice $10 $5
Changed notice $10 $5
Award notice $12 $7
Details from PDF $4 $2
Contract price from award $8 $4
Full-text search $3 $1

There is also a $0.05 charge per actor start. Bronze and Silver plans sit between the two columns. The README also lists a free starter allowance of 20 new notices, 10 detail downloads and 5 contract prices.

My run produced 17 new notices, 1 change, 12 awards, 20 PDF detail downloads and 9 contract prices. At Free plan prices that comes to roughly $0.53 for the whole week of IT tenders.

Responsible use

Public procurement data is public by law, and this actor reads the official UZP API rather than scraping HTML. That covers the tenders and the buying institutions.

Winners are a different matter. In Poland many small suppliers are sole traders, and their business name is often the owner's full name. In my run one of the winners was exactly that. Treat contractor names as personal data under GDPR: use them for the purpose you have a basis for (for example, competitive analysis inside your company), do not publish them in bulk, and do not build contact lists of individuals from them. The screenshot in this post masks the contractor name column for that reason.

This tutorial was written with AI assistance and checked by the author. All numbers come from a real run of the scraper.

title: When the product matches the background, the edge-hue test goes blind
summary:
The last post gated on a hue shift: composite the edge onto the shop's background, read its Lab hue, compare it to the product's own body, and call any shift inside ±10° clean.

That test has a hidden premise, and I listed five limitations at the end of that post without naming this one. It works because a white mug sits at hue 112° and the removed green screen sat at 150° — 38° of separation. Any green residue rotates the edge toward 150°, and 38° is far outside a ±10° band.

Take the separation away and the test has nothing to measure. Not "less to measure" — nothing. This post builds that case, because it isn't exotic: green packaging shot on a green screen, a blue bottle on a blue sweep, a beige catalogue page photographed on beige paper. All of those are real jobs. The cutouts I deal with at PicViva come from seller photos across exactly this range of setups, which is why I care whether the metric survives them.

Building the worst case

Same ground truth as before: the white ceramic mug, 1200×800, the Vision matte, one alpha shared by every variant — 9,959 partial-band pixels, 11,961 inner-ring pixels. Only the RGB changes.

To get a product that matches the background I recolour the subject. L* is untouched, so every highlight and shadow stays exactly where it was. Chroma is set to the background's hue and modulated by L*, so speculars wash out the way they do on a real glazed surface:

def dye(rgb, alpha, hue=HUE_G, chroma=40.0):
    lab = skc.rgb2lab(rgb / 255.0)
    L = lab[..., 0]
    lo, hi = L[alpha >= 250].min(), L[alpha >= 250].max()
    t = np.clip((L - lo) / (hi - lo), 0, 1)
    lab2 = lab.copy()
    lab2[..., 1] = chroma * (1 - 0.45 * t) * np.cos(np.radians(hue))
    lab2[..., 2] = chroma * (1 - 0.45 * t) * np.sin(np.radians(hue))
    return np.clip(skc.lab2rgb(lab2) * 255.0, 0, 255)

This is a synthetic dye job, not a photograph of a green mug — worth saying plainly. What it reproduces is a colour configuration, not a material: a subject whose body hue equals the hue of the background it was cut from. The rest of the geometry, the matte, the shading and the variant construction are unchanged from the previous two posts.

Two numbers set the experiment up:

background G          hue 150.2   C* 68.8
white mug body        hue 112.1   C* 2.20
  separation              38.1 deg

dyed product body     hue 150.6   C* 23.1
  separation              0.4 deg

0.4°. That is the whole experiment.

What the hue test reports

Same seven variants, same threshold, same code. Only the product colour moved.

Variant White ceramic Δhue Verdict Green ceramic Δhue Verdict
A clean −3.0 no colour cast +0.6 no colour cast
B raw blend +42.5 background colour present +4.2 no colour cast
C half despill +38.0 background colour present +3.0 no colour cast
D over-despill −114.2 pushed past neutral −3.1 no colour cast
E alpha grown −3.4 no colour cast +0.0 no colour cast
F thresholded +31.1 background colour present +1.1 no colour cast

Every verdict in the right-hand column is wrong except A and E. B is the extreme case: its edge is literally alpha·F + (1−alpha)·G, so its true background fraction is mean(1−alpha) = 0.498. Half the colour in half the band is background, and the test calls it clean at +4.2°.

Things I'd previously dismissed are now correct-by-accident in the worst way. D scores −3.1°, thirty-seven times closer to the body hue than its white-ceramic reading of −114.2° — not because it improved, but because there is no hue left to shift. And F, whose inner-ring spill of 0.085 the previous post found, drops to +1.1°.

Why it fails, and why widening the band won't help

If F and G share a hue, then any convex combination of them shares it too:

0.5·F + 0.5·G   has the hue of F, and of G, and of the mixture

An alpha blend is exactly that convex combination. So the hue of a contaminated edge is identical to the hue of a clean one — by construction, not by approximation. Dyeing the product to the background's hue doesn't weaken the signal, it deletes it.

That rules out the obvious response of shrinking the threshold. There is no threshold that separates two populations that coincide. It also explains the E and F rows landing near zero: those variants never had a hue shift to report, so nothing changed for them.

The useful conclusion is negative and cheap to state: the edge-hue test is valid only when the product and the background differ in hue. That's a precondition, not a tuning parameter, and it belongs in the docstring rather than in a limitations section.

What still works, attempt 1: the chroma ceiling

Go back to the reader suggestion from the last post — keep the edge colour inside the range of nearby opaque colours. I rejected it there because it couldn't separate C from D. But it was answering a different question, and that question comes back now: not which direction did the edge move, but did it move outside what the body explains.

Hue isn't available. Chroma might be. The background sits at C* 68.8; the body sits at C* 23.1. Any real blend of the two lands between them and is therefore more saturated than the body. That's a one-sided test, and one-sided is fine here as long as I'm clear about what it can't see.

Two versions of the ceiling — global, then per-pixel neighbourhood:

Variant global ceiling R=4 R=8 R=16 R=32
A clean 0.1% 23.2% 0.0% 0.0% 0.0%
B raw blend 6.9% 72.0% 46.1% 39.4% 31.1%
C half despill 0.4% 34.6% 10.2% 8.5% 6.6%
D over-despill 0.0% 23.2% 0.0% 0.0% 0.0%

(Percentages are the share of edge pixels above the ceiling. Global ceiling = body `C` p99.)*

The global ceiling is useless — 6.9% on B — because the body's own chroma spans up to p95 28.7, which is above most of B's edge band. The local version is a different story, but the radius matters more than I expected: at R=4 the neighbourhood is so small that the clean variant trips the gate on 23.2% of its own edge pixels, which is worse than useless in production.

R=8 is the first setting where the clean baseline is zero and B is caught at 46.1%. That's the shape of every one of these tests: a narrow radius is noisy, a wide radius is blind, and the clean baseline is what tells you which side of that trade you're on.

The ceiling has a saturation ceiling of its own

46.1% is already weak. It gets worse as the product gets more saturated, and the reason is arithmetic again.

The signal is fixed: the background contributes C* 68.8 no matter what. The noise is the body's own chroma p95, which grows with the product's saturation. When the body's ceiling climbs above the contaminated edge's chroma, the test can't see the contamination at all.

Product C* (nominal) body C* mean body p95 B edge C* B above ceiling
12 7.1 8.6 13.1 76.3%
20 11.7 14.3 14.8 58.0%
30 17.5 21.5 16.8 30.1%
40 23.1 28.7 18.9 6.9%
55 31.6 39.4 22.0 0.4%

The clean baseline stays at 0.1% throughout, so this isn't noise — it's the ceiling genuinely rising past the signal. Note the crossing between rows 3 and 4: body p95 (21.5 → 28.7) overtakes B edge C* (16.8 → 18.9), and the catch rate falls from 30.1% to 6.9% in one step. A pale green product is detectable; a saturated one is not.

That's not a fixable weakness of this particular test. If the product and the background have the same hue and comparable saturation, a residue of the background is genuinely indistinguishable from the product — by eye or by any colour statistic. The image contains less information, and no formula recovers it.

What still works, attempt 2: the signed chroma residual

The ceiling only catches contamination that raises chroma. It leaves D — over-despill — invisible, and D is the failure mode this whole series started with. So I tried one more thing: instead of a ceiling, predict the chroma.

A pure alpha blend of F onto white has a predictable chroma given the alpha. I don't know F per pixel, but I know the body's mean Lab, which is one number available on any cutout. Feed that in and compare:

mean_lab = lab_body[body].mean(0)          # the body, one colour
white_lab = rgb2lab([[255, 255, 255]])/255.

a = alpha[mask] / 255.0
expected = a*mean_lab + (1-a)*white_lab    # what a clean blend would look like
C_expected = hypot(expected[:, 1], expected[:, 2])
residual = C_actual[mask] - C_expected
Variant edge C* expected C* residual pixels below −3 above +3
A clean 11.65 11.60 +0.05 14.6% 12.7%
B raw blend 18.89 11.60 +7.29 2.5% 82.7%
C half despill 15.27 11.60 +3.67 4.5% 61.5%
D over-despill 7.89 11.60 −3.71 51.1% 4.1%

This works better than the ceiling for the thing I actually need. The sign is the diagnosis: +7.29 is background still in the edge, −3.71 is the edge pushed below what the product can explain — over-despill. B and D land on opposite sides of the clean baseline, which is exactly the discrimination the hue test delivered in the white-ceramic case and loses here.

The cost is a wider baseline. The clean variant has 14.6% of its edge pixels below −3 and 12.7% above +3, because the body mean is a crude stand-in for whatever F really is at a given edge pixel. That's a real precision loss: the same gate on white ceramic had a clean baseline of ±3° in hue, not a 27% false-positive rate in chroma.

Still, the mean residual separates cleanly (+0.05 / +7.29 / +3.67 / −3.71) with no reference image and no knowledge of G. For a build gate that reports "this cutout's edge band is 7.3 chroma units more saturated than its body allows", that's enough to act on.

The channel I expected to work, and didn't

Luminance looked like the obvious third option. The background is L* 72.9, the body is L* 86.0, so a blend should darken the edge. Small, but measurable — and unlike hue and chroma, L* doesn't depend on the product being unsaturated.

It doesn't survive the object's own shading:

Variant L* residual p5 p95
A clean −1.8 −20.1 +9.9
B raw blend −3.6 −19.1 +7.2
C half despill −2.7 −19.7 +8.5
D over-despill −1.2 −20.7 +10.6

The body's L* spans 40 to 97 — rim shading, curvature, the handle's shadow. Edge pixels legitimately sit 20 levels below the body mean, roughly ten times the 1.8-level gap between clean and raw-blend. L* is the noisiest channel at a cutout boundary, not a spare one. I'm recording it because it's the intuitive next guess and it wastes an afternoon.

Where this leaves the test

Put the two posts together and the condition is explicit:

The edge-hue test (previous post) applies when the product and background differ in hue. White product on green screen, white on blue, metal on beige — the common cases. It gives a clean, interpretable sign and a tight baseline.

When they don't differ, the signed chroma residual applies — worse baseline, one-sided in practice, but it separates B from D and needs only the image.

When they don't differ and the product is saturated, neither is reliable, and the honest move is to go back to a metric that knows G. Spill fraction from the first post costs you the source background colour, and if you're cutting from a controlled sweep you already have it. Paying that cost beats shipping on a statistic that reports 0.4% on a cutout where half the edge is background.

The transferable part isn't the threshold or the formula. It's that every reference-free metric is trading a known input for statistical luck, and each one has a region where that luck runs out. Finding the region is more useful than the metric.

If you gate cutout quality in a pipeline, do you know where yours stops working? The cheap version of that answer is one afternoon: take a paid cutout, degrade it the way your pipeline degrades, dye the subject to match its background, and re-run your gate. If the verdicts don't change, the gate is measuring the subject's colour, not the edge.

Put the two posts together and the condition is explicit:

The edge-hue test (previous post) applies when the product and background differ in hue. White product on green screen, white on blue, metal on beige — the common cases. It gives a clean, interpretable sign and a tight baseline.

When they don't differ, the signed chroma residual applies — worse baseline, one-sided in practice, but it separates B from D and needs only the image.

When they don't differ and the product is saturated, neither is reliable, and the honest move is to go back to a metric that knows G. Spill fraction from the first post costs you the source background colour, and if you're cutting from a controlled sweep you already have it. Paying that cost beats shipping on a statistic that reports 0.4% on a cutout where half the edge is background.

The transferable part isn't the threshold or the formula. It's that every reference-free metric is trading a known input for statistical luck, and each one has a region where that luck runs out. Finding the region is more useful than the metric.

If you gate cutout quality in a pipeline, do you know where yours stops working? The cheap version of that answer is one afternoon: take a paid cutout, degrade it the way your pipeline degrades, dye the subject to match its background, and re-run your gate. If the verdicts don't change, the gate is measuring the subject's colour, not the edge.

title: "Prime Number and Non-Prime Number Checking Using Loops"
summary:
1. Divide the Tiles Equally Problem: A school is preparing a large square floor for its annual function. The floor has N tiles arranged in a single row. The teacher wants to divide these tiles into equal-sized groups without leaving any tile unused. For example, if there are 12 tiles, the teacher can make:

1 group of 12 tiles
2 groups of 6 tiles
3 groups of 4 tiles
4 groups of 3 tiles
6 groups of 2 tiles
12 groups of 1 tile

Write a Python program that takes the number of tiles N and finds all possible group sizes that can divide the tiles equally.
1*12=12 # Remaining 0
2*6=12 # Remaining 0
3*4=12 # Remaining 0
4*3=12 # Remaining 0
5*2=10 # Remaining !=0
6*2=12 # Remaining 0
The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12 are called Divisors.

Step 1: Without a Loop

no = 12
if no % 1 == 0:
    print(1)
if no % 2 == 0:
    print(2)
if no % 3 == 0:
    print(3)
if no % 4 == 0:
    print(4)
if no % 5 == 0:
    print(5)

This approach requires writing multiple if conditions.

Step 2: We define a variable
we can use a variable called divisor.

no = 12
divisor = 1
while divisor <= no:
    if no % divisor == 0:
        print(divisor)
    divisor = divisor + 1

Output:

1
2
3
4
6
12
Step 3: Optimizing the Loop
The biggest proper divisor of a number cannot be greater than half of that number.

For example:

8 → 4
20 → 10
1000 → 500
10000 → 5000

We can exclude the number itself and check only up to no // 2.

no = 12
divisor = 1
while divisor <= no//2:
    if no % divisor == 0:
        print(divisor)
    divisor = divisor + 1

2
3
4
6

special_number=0
print("special_number :", end=" ")  
while no <20:
    divisor=2
    while divisor <=no//2:
        if no%divisor==0:
            break
        divisor+=1
    else:
        print(no,end=" ")
    no+=1

title: Track RemoteOK jobs in SQL without counting timestamps as salary edits
summary:
Your weekly salary chart has moved upwards. Before you publish “employers raised pay”, you need to establish whether any repeatedly observed listing changed its advertised range.

The Remote OK Actor merges feeds and deduplicates listings by jobId. It also adds scrapedAt, while salary fields can be absent. Comparing entire records would therefore count collection timestamps as edits; comparing aggregate salaries would mix edits with changing membership.

Matching snapshots on jobId separates salary-band revisions on repeatedly observed listings from changes in the observed listing mix.

What actually moved in your salary chart?

The awkward moment comes when your manager asks which employers changed their bands, and your aggregate query can't name a listing.

An average can rise because lower-paid listings disappeared from your sample. It can also rise because higher-paid listings became observable, including listings whose salary was previously missing.

Neither mechanism requires an existing advertised range to change.

Example collection settings keep listings without salaries and hold enrichment constant, so missing pay remains visible to the analysis:

import os
import json
import re
import math
from decimal import Decimal
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from uuid import uuid4

import pandas as pd
import duckdb
from apify_client import ApifyClient

client = ApifyClient(os.environ["APIFY_TOKEN"])
run_input = {
    "mode": "byTags",
    "tags": ["python", "data-science"],
    "region": "any",
    "salaryOnly": False,
    "enrichDetails": True,
    "maxItems": 1000,
}

Many listings publish salary only on their job page, which enrichment fetches. Switching that setting between captures can make salary appear without an employer editing anything.

We also leave salary thresholds out of this comparison. Otherwise, a revised band could push a listing across your filter boundary and turn a content change into an apparent arrival or disappearance.

The useful split looks like this:

Earlier snapshot ── jobId match ── Later snapshot
                       │
           ┌───────────┼────────────┐
        matched    newly observed   absent later
           │
    comparable salary evidence
           │
    changed or unchanged band

Those branches answer different questions. Your chart shouldn't quietly fold them into the same explanation.

Use the listing ID, not the job title

Use jobId for membership and (snapshot_id, job_id) for stored-row uniqueness.

A company can advertise several similarly named roles. A title can change while the listing remains identifiable. Joining on company and title can manufacture both departures and arrivals.

Normalise the ID before storage. An integer representation and its equivalent string shouldn't become separate listings.

The salary parser below accepts numeric values and conventional currency-prefixed, comma-grouped strings. It rejects unfamiliar formats rather than guessing what they mean:

def normalise_id(value):
    if value is None or isinstance(value, bool):
        raise ValueError("Missing or invalid jobId")
    number = Decimal(str(value).strip())
    if not number.is_finite() or number != number.to_integral_value():
        raise ValueError("jobId must be an integer identifier")
    return str(int(number))

def parse_salary(value):
    if value is None:
        return None
    text = str(value).strip()
    if not text:
        return None
    text = re.sub(r"^(?:USD\s*|\$\s*)", "", text, flags=re.I)
    if not re.fullmatch(r"(?:\d{1,3}(?:,\d{3})+|\d+)(?:\.\d+)?", text):
        raise ValueError(f"Unrecognised salary format: {value!r}")
    amount = float(text.replace(",", ""))
    if not math.isfinite(amount):
        raise ValueError("Salary must be finite")
    return amount

Empty fields are omitted from records, so extraction uses .get() explicitly.

A missing endpoint stays missing. It doesn't become zero, an open-ended range, or a value borrowed from the previous capture. Each substitution would create a different salary measure.

Keep each capture and its settings

Store a snapshot manifest separately from its listings. Otherwise, an empty capture has no rows and quietly loses its existence.

Keep the raw observations alongside the normalised endpoints. That gives you somewhere to investigate an apparent revision without making every optional field part of the comparison.

These tables enforce unique snapshot membership and define which rows qualify for the salary calculation:

con = duckdb.connect()
con.execute("""
CREATE TABLE snapshots (
    snapshot_id VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY,
    captured_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL,
    settings_json VARCHAR NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE listings (
    snapshot_id VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    job_id VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    salary_min DOUBLE,
    salary_max DOUBLE,
    currency VARCHAR,
    raw_json VARCHAR NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (snapshot_id, job_id)
);

CREATE VIEW salary_rows AS
SELECT *,
       COALESCE(
           currency = 'USD'
           AND salary_min >= 0
           AND salary_min <= salary_max,
           FALSE
       ) AS salary_ok
FROM listings;
""").fetchall()

Here, a comparable salary requires both endpoints, an explicit USD currency and an ordered, non-negative range. A partial band may still contain useful information, but it doesn't enter this particular midpoint measure.

The notebook uses memory for storage. A weekly tracker needs these same tables retained in persistent storage between scheduled captures.

At ingestion, repeated observations of an ID become a single membership row. If their normalised salary tuples disagree within that capture, we retain every raw observation and leave the analytical tuple empty: choosing whichever arrived last would manufacture certainty.

This function reconciles those observations, validates membership in SQL, then writes the manifest and its batch atomically:

def capture(settings):
    settings_json = json.dumps(settings, sort_keys=True)
    run = client.actor(
        "dataspryva/remoteok-job-board-tag-and-region-filter-tool"
    ).call(run_input=settings)
    if run["status"] != "SUCCEEDED":
        raise RuntimeError(f"Capture failed: {run['status']}")

    grouped = {}
    for item in client.dataset(run["defaultDatasetId"]).iterate_items():
        job_id = normalise_id(item.get("jobId"))
        currency = item.get("salaryCurrency")
        band = (
            parse_salary(item.get("salaryMin")),
            parse_salary(item.get("salaryMax")),
            str(currency).strip().upper() if currency else None,
        )
        observations = grouped.setdefault(
            job_id, {"bands": set(), "records": []}
        )
        observations["bands"].add(band)
        observations["records"].append(item)

    rows = []
    for job_id, observations in grouped.items():
        band = (
            next(iter(observations["bands"]))
            if len(observations["bands"]) == 1
            else (None, None, None)
        )
        rows.append({
            "job_id": job_id,
            "salary_min": band[0],
            "salary_max": band[1],
            "currency": band[2],
            "raw_json": json.dumps(
                observations["records"], sort_keys=True
            ),
        })

    batch = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=[
        "job_id", "salary_min", "salary_max", "currency", "raw_json"
    ])
    con.register("incoming", batch)
    try:
        duplicates = con.execute("""
            SELECT job_id FROM incoming
            GROUP BY job_id HAVING count(*) > 1
        """).fetchall()
        if duplicates:
            raise ValueError("Duplicate jobId after reconciliation")

        snapshot_id = str(uuid4())
        con.execute("BEGIN").fetchall()
        try:
            con.execute(
                "INSERT INTO snapshots VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                [snapshot_id, datetime.now(timezone.utc), settings_json],
            ).fetchall()
            con.execute("""
                INSERT INTO listings
                SELECT ?, job_id, salary_min, salary_max, currency, raw_json
                FROM incoming
            """, [snapshot_id]).fetchall()
            con.execute("COMMIT").fetchall()
        except Exception:
            con.execute("ROLLBACK").fetchall()
            raise
    finally:
        con.unregister("incoming")
    return snapshot_id

before_id = capture(run_input)
after_id = capture(run_input)

The adjacent calls collect successive observations; they don't represent a weekly interval. For weekly reporting, use the retained snapshot IDs from that interval.

There's deliberately no update path here. Overwriting an earlier salary would remove the evidence needed to explain its revision.

Join snapshots before comparing salaries

A full outer join preserves arrivals and disappearances. An inner join would remove precisely the membership changes you're trying to distinguish.

First reject differing collection settings. Then classify matched listings only when both observations have comparable salary evidence:

settings_count = con.execute("""
    SELECT count(DISTINCT settings_json)
    FROM snapshots
    WHERE snapshot_id IN (?, ?)
""", [before_id, after_id]).fetchall()[0][0]
if settings_count != 1:
    raise ValueError("Collection settings differ between snapshots")

con.execute("""
CREATE TABLE comparison AS
WITH earlier AS (
    SELECT * FROM salary_rows WHERE snapshot_id = ?
), later AS (
    SELECT * FROM salary_rows WHERE snapshot_id = ?
), paired AS (
    SELECT
        job_id,
        earlier.snapshot_id IS NOT NULL AS seen_before,
        later.snapshot_id IS NOT NULL AS seen_after,
        earlier.salary_ok AS old_ok,
        later.salary_ok AS new_ok,
        earlier.salary_min AS old_min,
        earlier.salary_max AS old_max,
        earlier.currency AS old_currency,
        later.salary_min AS new_min,
        later.salary_max AS new_max,
        later.currency AS new_currency
    FROM earlier FULL OUTER JOIN later USING (job_id)
)
SELECT *,
    CASE
        WHEN NOT seen_before THEN 'newly_observed'
        WHEN NOT seen_after THEN 'not_observed_again'
        WHEN NOT (old_ok AND new_ok) THEN 'salary_not_comparable'
        WHEN (old_min, old_max, old_currency)
             IS DISTINCT FROM (new_min, new_max, new_currency)
            THEN 'band_changed'
        ELSE 'band_unchanged'
    END AS status
FROM paired
""", [before_id, after_id]).fetchall()

The tuple comparison is null-safe, but null safety alone doesn't establish comparability. That's why the salary-evidence check comes first.

A listing gaining a complete salary range belongs in an observability investigation. Treating its previous missing range as zero would give your chart a very enthusiastic fictional pay rise.

Count arrivals separately from salary edits

Keep the full snapshot summary, the membership ledger and the matched salary calculation separate.

These queries produce pandas tables without combining those measures:

snapshot_summary = con.execute("""
    SELECT
        s.snapshot_id,
        count(l.job_id) AS observed_listings,
        count(l.job_id) FILTER (WHERE l.salary_ok) AS comparable_salary_rows,
        avg((l.salary_min + l.salary_max) / 2)
            FILTER (WHERE l.salary_ok) AS mean_band_midpoint
    FROM snapshots s
    LEFT JOIN salary_rows l USING (snapshot_id)
    WHERE s.snapshot_id IN (?, ?)
    GROUP BY s.snapshot_id
""", [before_id, after_id]).df()

membership_summary = con.execute("""
    SELECT status, count(*) AS listings
    FROM comparison
    GROUP BY status
""").df()

matched_summary = con.execute("""
    SELECT
        count(*) AS comparable_matches,
        count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'band_changed') AS changed_bands,
        avg(
            ((new_min + new_max) - (old_min + old_max)) / 2
        ) AS mean_midpoint_change
    FROM comparison
    WHERE status IN ('band_changed', 'band_unchanged')
""").df()

The matched mean includes unchanged bands. Restricting it to edited listings would answer how large revisions were among revision candidates, rather than how the repeatedly observed comparable listings moved overall.

The midpoint is a deliberately named summary of advertised endpoints. It isn't an expected offer.

Nor is this an additive decomposition of the aggregate movement. Changing membership and changing salary observability can alter the denominator, so subtracting the matched mean change from the full-chart change doesn't produce a clean “composition effect”.

Separate extraction noise from revision candidates

The useful comparison boundary is narrower than “anything in the JSON changed”.

Field or setting Treatment Analytical consequence
salaryMin, salaryMax, salaryCurrency Compare the normalised tuple after eligibility checks Flags observed band revisions
scrapedAt Retain as collection metadata A fresh capture is not a content edit
postedAt Retain separately from collection time Posting time does not date a salary revision
mode, input tags, region, maxItems Hold constant and save in the manifest Selection changes can alter membership
enrichDetails Hold constant Different extraction depth can alter salary visibility

Identical settings are necessary for this comparison, but they aren't proof that extraction conditions were identical. A missing endpoint remains ambiguous until you inspect the underlying evidence.

Even a complete-to-complete change is initially a revision candidate. Before attributing it to an employer, inspect the raw records and the listing page. The stored capture times bound when you observed the difference; they don't establish when the underlying edit happened.

Keep the full chart beside the matched panel

The worked source is our RemoteOK Job Board Tag & Region Filter Tool.

Its feed slices contain about 100 latest jobs per tag and offer no pagination. Combining tags broadens the observed set, but doesn't create a census.

That matters for disappearances: a listing can leave your observed feed without leaving the board. Reaching maxItems adds another selection boundary. Raising that cap can't recover records the source feed never exposed.

Label the comparison accordingly: newly observed, rather than newly created; not observed again, rather than filled.

The matched panel has its own selection effect. It retains listings visible at both capture points, with usable salary evidence at both. Listings that persist may differ from those that turn over quickly.

Your full snapshot chart describes the observed inventory. Your matched calculation describes changes within its repeatedly observed, salary-comparable subset. Keeping both visible makes the limitation inspectable.

A listing isn't a payslip

A jobId identifies an advertised listing. It doesn't establish a unique hiring position, headcount, an accepted offer or anyone's realised earnings.

Even if both endpoints rise for a matched listing, you've evidence of an observed advertised-band revision, subject to checking extraction. You haven't measured wage growth.

The defensible sentence names the evidence: the observed inventory changed, particular matched bands changed, or both.

A rising line can't choose that sentence for you.

            con.execute(
                "INSERT INTO snapshots VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                [snapshot_id, datetime.now(timezone.utc), settings_json],
            ).fetchall()
            con.execute("""
                INSERT INTO listings
                SELECT ?, job_id, salary_min, salary_max, currency, raw_json
                FROM incoming
            """, [snapshot_id]).fetchall()
            con.execute("COMMIT").fetchall()
        except Exception:
            con.execute("ROLLBACK").fetchall()
            raise
    finally:
        con.unregister("incoming")
    return snapshot_id

before_id = capture(run_input)
after_id = capture(run_input)

The adjacent calls collect successive observations; they don't represent a weekly interval. For weekly reporting, use the retained snapshot IDs from that interval.

There's deliberately no update path here. Overwriting an earlier salary would remove the evidence needed to explain its revision.

Join snapshots before comparing salaries

A full outer join preserves arrivals and disappearances. An inner join would remove precisely the membership changes you're trying to distinguish.

First reject differing collection settings. Then classify matched listings only when both observations have comparable salary evidence:

settings_count = con.execute("""
    SELECT count(DISTINCT settings_json)
    FROM snapshots
    WHERE snapshot_id IN (?, ?)
""", [before_id, after_id]).fetchall()[0][0]
if settings_count != 1:
    raise ValueError("Collection settings differ between snapshots")

con.execute("""
CREATE TABLE comparison AS
WITH earlier AS (
    SELECT * FROM salary_rows WHERE snapshot_id = ?
), later AS (
    SELECT * FROM salary_rows WHERE snapshot_id = ?
), paired AS (
    SELECT
        job_id,
        earlier.snapshot_id IS NOT NULL AS seen_before,
        later.snapshot_id IS NOT NULL AS seen_after,
        earlier.salary_ok AS old_ok,
        later.salary_ok AS new_ok,
        earlier.salary_min AS old_min,
        earlier.salary_max AS old_max,
        earlier.currency AS old_currency,
        later.salary_min AS new_min,
        later.salary_max AS new_max,
        later.currency AS new_currency
    FROM earlier FULL OUTER JOIN later USING (job_id)
)
SELECT *,
    CASE
        WHEN NOT seen_before THEN 'newly_observed'
        WHEN NOT seen_after THEN 'not_observed_again'
        WHEN NOT (old_ok AND new_ok) THEN 'salary_not_comparable'
        WHEN (old_min, old_max, old_currency)
             IS DISTINCT FROM (new_min, new_max, new_currency)
            THEN 'band_changed'
        ELSE 'band_unchanged'
    END AS status
FROM paired
""", [before_id, after_id]).fetchall()

The tuple comparison is null-safe, but null safety alone doesn't establish comparability. That's why the salary-evidence check comes first.

A listing gaining a complete salary range belongs in an observability investigation. Treating its previous missing range as zero would give your chart a very enthusiastic fictional pay rise.

Count arrivals separately from salary edits

Keep the full snapshot summary, the membership ledger and the matched salary calculation separate.

These queries produce pandas tables without combining those measures:

snapshot_summary = con.execute("""
    SELECT
        s.snapshot_id,
        count(l.job_id) AS observed_listings,
        count(l.job_id) FILTER (WHERE l.salary_ok) AS comparable_salary_rows,
        avg((l.salary_min + l.salary_max) / 2)
            FILTER (WHERE l.salary_ok) AS mean_band_midpoint
    FROM snapshots s
    LEFT JOIN salary_rows l USING (snapshot_id)
    WHERE s.snapshot_id IN (?, ?)
    GROUP BY s.snapshot_id
""", [before_id, after_id]).df()

membership_summary = con.execute("""
    SELECT status, count(*) AS listings
    FROM comparison
    GROUP BY status
""").df()

matched_summary = con.execute("""
    SELECT
        count(*) AS comparable_matches,
        count(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'band_changed') AS changed_bands,
        avg(
            ((new_min + new_max) - (old_min + old_max)) / 2
        ) AS mean_midpoint_change
    FROM comparison
    WHERE status IN ('band_changed', 'band_unchanged')
""").df()

The matched mean includes unchanged bands. Restricting it to edited listings would answer how large revisions were among revision candidates, rather than how the repeatedly observed comparable listings moved overall.

The midpoint is a deliberately named summary of advertised endpoints. It isn't an expected offer.

Nor is this an additive decomposition of the aggregate movement. Changing membership and changing salary observability can alter the denominator, so subtracting the matched mean change from the full-chart change doesn't produce a clean “composition effect”.

Separate extraction noise from revision candidates

The useful comparison boundary is narrower than “anything in the JSON changed”.

Field or setting Treatment Analytical consequence
salaryMin, salaryMax, salaryCurrency Compare the normalised tuple after eligibility checks Flags observed band revisions
scrapedAt Retain as collection metadata A fresh capture is not a content edit
postedAt Retain separately from collection time Posting time does not date a salary revision
mode, input tags, region, maxItems Hold constant and save in the manifest Selection changes can alter membership
enrichDetails Hold constant Different extraction depth can alter salary visibility

Identical settings are necessary for this comparison, but they aren't proof that extraction conditions were identical. A missing endpoint remains ambiguous until you inspect the underlying evidence.

Even a complete-to-complete change is initially a revision candidate. Before attributing it to an employer, inspect the raw records and the listing page. The stored capture times bound when you observed the difference; they don't establish when the underlying edit happened.

Keep the full chart beside the matched panel

The worked source is our RemoteOK Job Board Tag & Region Filter Tool.

Its feed slices contain about 100 latest jobs per tag and offer no pagination. Combining tags broadens the observed set, but doesn't create a census.

That matters for disappearances: a listing can leave your observed feed without leaving the board. Reaching maxItems adds another selection boundary. Raising that cap can't recover records the source feed never exposed.

Label the comparison accordingly: newly observed, rather than newly created; not observed again, rather than filled.

The matched panel has its own selection effect. It retains listings visible at both capture points, with usable salary evidence at both. Listings that persist may differ from those that turn over quickly.

Your full snapshot chart describes the observed inventory. Your matched calculation describes changes within its repeatedly observed, salary-comparable subset. Keeping both visible makes the limitation inspectable.

A listing isn't a payslip

A jobId identifies an advertised listing. It doesn't establish a unique hiring position, headcount, an accepted offer or anyone's realised earnings.

Even if both endpoints rise for a matched listing, you've evidence of an observed advertised-band revision, subject to checking extraction. You haven't measured wage growth.

The defensible sentence names the evidence: the observed inventory changed, particular matched bands changed, or both.

A rising line can't choose that sentence for you.
